Write a number from 1 to 3999 in Roman numerals.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/roman-numerals) (MIT). Listed under [Encoding & Ciphers](/examples/?subject=encoding-and-ciphers).

```nomi-run
// FILE: roman_numerals.nomi
once numerals = [
    #(1000, "M"),
    #(900, "CM"),
    #(500, "D"),
    #(400, "CD"),
    #(100, "C"),
    #(90, "XC"),
    #(50, "L"),
    #(40, "XL"),
    #(10, "X"),
    #(9, "IX"),
    #(5, "V"),
    #(4, "IV"),
    #(1, "I"),
]

/// `number` in Roman numerals. Each numeral, largest first, is written as
/// many times as it fits into what is left.
pub fn roman(number: Int) -> String {
    #(parts, _left) = Iter.map_reduce(numerals, fn left = number, #(value, symbol) -> {
        #(String.repeat(symbol, left / value), left % value)
    })

    String.join(parts)
}

// FILE: roman_numerals_test.nomi
import roman_numerals

test "converts to Roman numerals" {
    cases = [
        #("1 is I", 1, "I"),
        #("2 is II", 2, "II"),
        #("3 is III", 3, "III"),
        #("4 is IV", 4, "IV"),
        #("5 is V", 5, "V"),
        #("6 is VI", 6, "VI"),
        #("9 is IX", 9, "IX"),
        #("16 is XVI", 16, "XVI"),
        #("27 is XXVII", 27, "XXVII"),
        #("48 is XLVIII", 48, "XLVIII"),
        #("49 is XLIX", 49, "XLIX"),
        #("59 is LIX", 59, "LIX"),
        #("66 is LXVI", 66, "LXVI"),
        #("93 is XCIII", 93, "XCIII"),
        #("141 is CXLI", 141, "CXLI"),
        #("163 is CLXIII", 163, "CLXIII"),
        #("166 is CLXVI", 166, "CLXVI"),
        #("402 is CDII", 402, "CDII"),
        #("575 is DLXXV", 575, "DLXXV"),
        #("666 is DCLXVI", 666, "DCLXVI"),
        #("911 is CMXI", 911, "CMXI"),
        #("1024 is MXXIV", 1024, "MXXIV"),
        #("1666 is MDCLXVI", 1666, "MDCLXVI"),
        #("3000 is MMM", 3000, "MMM"),
        #("3001 is MMMI", 3001, "MMMI"),
        #("3888 is MMMDCCCLXXXVIII", 3888, "MMMDCCCLXXXVIII"),
        #("3999 is MMMCMXCIX", 3999, "MMMCMXCIX"),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, number, expected), description {
        assert roman_numerals.roman(number) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The numerals, subtractive pairs included, are a `once` table of `#(value, symbol)` tuples, largest first.
- One `Iter.map_reduce` over the table: each numeral's output is its symbol repeated `left / value` times, and the state carried to the next is `left % value`. The parts are joined with `String.join`. An `Iter.reduce` threading `#(left, text)` and concatenating was the other form; style §27 picks `map_reduce` when each element has its own output and the state only carries what the next one needs.
- No validation of the range, since the canonical data has no error cases.
- One `subtests` table for all 27 cases.
